summary: Updates the specification of CUBIC, a TCP congestion control algorithm that grows the window with a cubic function, to include improvements from implementations and academic work. It is the default in Linux, Windows, and Apple stacks.

plainLanguage.summary: CUBIC decides how fast a TCP connection may send. After a packet is lost, the old method, called Reno, adds only one packet to the sending window per round trip, which is far too slow on a fast link with a long delay. CUBIC instead grows the window with a cubic curve of the time since the loss, so a long link fills quickly and short links keep the old behaviour. On a loss it keeps 0.7 of the window instead of Reno's half.

what is the cubic c constant
subtitle: The TCP congestion control algorithm that grows its sending window with a cubic function.

tldr.problem: The classic Reno congestion control algorithm grows its sending window one segment per round-trip time, so on a fast link with a long delay it takes a very long time to fill the pipe again after a loss.
tldr.mechanism: CUBIC grows the window with a cubic function of the time since the last congestion event, using a concave profile up to the window size at which the last loss happened and a convex profile after it. A separate estimate keeps Reno-like growth on short-delay paths, and the window is cut to 0.7 of its size on a loss.
tldr.outcome: This document moved CUBIC to the Standards Track, replacing RFC 8312, and updated RFC 5681 so that CUBIC's more aggressive window growth is permitted. It also records the value 0.4 for the constant C as the recommended setting.

today: RFC 9438 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 8312, the earlier CUBIC specification, and updates RFC 5681, the base TCP congestion control specification. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why CUBIC Exists
sections.content:
CUBIC has been adopted as the default TCP congestion control algorithm in the Linux, Windows and Apple stacks and has been deployed globally. A decade of deployment experience in very different Internet scenarios has shown that CUBIC is safe for deployment on the global Internet and delivers substantial benefits over classical Reno congestion control. It is therefore the most widely deployed standard for TCP congestion control, and it can also be used as the default congestion controller for other transport protocols such as QUIC and SCTP.

The design of CUBIC was motivated by the well-documented problem classical Reno TCP has with low utilization over fast and long-distance networks. The problem comes from a slow increase of the congestion window after a congestion event in a network with a large bandwidth-delay product, and it is often observed even at window sizes of several hundred packets. The same problem applies to all Reno-style standards, which this document collectively calls Reno.

CUBIC modifies the congestion control algorithm of classical Reno by using a cubic function instead of the linear window increase function of Reno, which improves scalability and stability over fast and long-distance networks. It is designed to be less aggressive and fairer to Reno in bandwidth usage than Binary Increase Congestion Control, its predecessor, while keeping that algorithm's strengths such as stability, window scalability and RTT-fairness.

This document updates the specification of CUBIC with algorithmic improvements taken from the Linux, Windows and Apple implementations and from recent academic work. It also moves the specification to the Standards Track, replacing the earlier CUBIC RFC. Because CUBIC is occasionally more aggressive than the algorithms in the base TCP congestion control specification, that document is updated as well: CUBIC may increase the congestion window by more than one segment per round-trip time during congestion avoidance, and it recommends the HyStart++ algorithm for slow start, which also allows increases of more than one segment per acknowledgement.
sections.plainLanguage: Reno adds one packet to the sending window per round trip. On a link with a long delay that is far too slow, and the link stays underused. CUBIC replaces that with a curve that grows quickly after a long idle period and settles down again near the point where the last loss happened.

sections.title: The Four Design Principles
sections.content:
CUBIC is designed on four principles.

The first is about the shape of the increase function. For better network utilisation and stability, CUBIC uses both the concave and the convex profiles of a cubic function to increase the congestion window, rather than only a convex one. After a window reduction, CUBIC remembers the window size at which it received the congestion event and performs a multiplicative decrease. When it enters congestion avoidance it starts with the concave profile, with the cubic function set so that its plateau is at the remembered window size, so the concave increase continues until then. After that the function turns convex and the convex increase begins. The window stays almost constant around the remembered size, where network utilisation is deemed highest, and under steady state most window samples sit close to it. Algorithms that use only a convex function have their largest increments around that same point, which produces many packet bursts near the saturation point and likely frequent global loss synchronisations.

The second principle is Reno-friendliness: CUBIC should behave like Reno on short-RTT, small-bandwidth networks where Reno performs well. An algorithm friendly to Reno per flow must increase its window less aggressively in small-BDP networks than in large-BDP ones, and CUBIC's aggressiveness depends mostly on the maximum window size before a reduction, which is smaller in small-BDP networks. Where the cubic function would increase the window less aggressively than Reno, CUBIC simply follows Reno's window size, so it achieves at least the same throughput. That region is called the Reno-friendly region.

The third principle is RTT-fairness: CUBIC should achieve linear bandwidth sharing among flows with different RTTs. Outside the Reno-friendly region the window increase rate does not depend on the RTT, so flows with different RTTs end up with similar window sizes in steady state, and their throughput ratio is proportional to the inverse of their RTT ratio. Reno gives the same linear ratio under an asynchronous loss model, but a quadratic ratio under a synchronous one.

The fourth principle sets the decrease factor. To balance scalability against convergence speed, CUBIC sets its multiplicative window decrease factor to 0.7, where Reno uses 0.5. The side effect is slower convergence, especially under low statistical multiplexing, but the Internet becomes more asynchronous with less frequent loss synchronisations as statistical multiplexing grows, and in such environments even strict multiplicative-increase multiplicative-decrease can converge. CUBIC flows with the same RTT always converge to the same throughput, independently of statistical multiplexing.
sections.plainLanguage: The four rules are: use both halves of a cubic curve, behave like Reno on short paths, share bandwidth evenly between short and long paths, and cut the window to 0.7 rather than half on a loss. The last choice makes the algorithm scale better but converge more slowly.

sections.title: The Cubic Increase Function
sections.content:
The unit of all window sizes in the document is segments of the sender maximum segment size, and the unit of all times is seconds. An implementation may use bytes instead, factoring in the segment size wherever needed.

CUBIC keeps the ACK clocking of Reno, increasing the congestion window only when a new acknowledgement arrives, and it makes no changes to the fast recovery and fast retransmit algorithms. During congestion avoidance it uses its own increase function, the cubic W_cubic(t) = C * (t - K)^3 + W_max, where t is the elapsed time in seconds since the current congestion avoidance stage began, that is the current time minus t_epoch. K is the time the function takes to raise the window to W_max from the start of the stage, and it is the cube root of (W_max minus cwnd_epoch) divided by C.

On each new acknowledgement CUBIC computes the target window size for the next round trip, W_cubic(t + RTT), with lower and upper bounds so that the increase rate is non-decreasing and slower than the slow start increase rate: the target is cwnd if the cubic value is below cwnd, 1.5 times cwnd if the cubic value is above 1.5 times cwnd, and the cubic value otherwise. The elapsed time t must not include periods when cwnd was not updated because the application had nothing to send.

The constants are the decrease factor beta_cubic, the additive increase factor alpha_cubic used in the Reno-friendly region, and C, a constant that determines how aggressive CUBIC is against other algorithms in high-BDP networks. The unit for C is segment per second cubed. The variables are the smoothed round-trip time, the current window, the slow start threshold, cwnd_prior, the window size when the threshold was last set, W_max, the window size just before the last reduction, K, the time period for the cubic function to reach W_max, the current time, the time and window size at the start of the current stage, W_cubic(t), the target, W_est, an estimate of Reno's window in the Reno-friendly region, and segments_acked, the number of segments acknowledged by a new acknowledgement.
sections.plainLanguage: The window grows along a cubic curve of the time since the last loss, shifted so the flat part of the curve sits at the window size that caused the loss. K is the time at which the curve reaches that size, worked out from the curve's own constant C.

sections.title: The Reno-Friendly, Concave and Convex Regions
sections.content:
Depending on the value of the current window, CUBIC runs in three regions. In the Reno-friendly region it ensures at least the same throughput as Reno. In the concave region, used when CUBIC is not Reno-friendly and cwnd is below W_max, the window is increased by (target minus cwnd) divided by cwnd for each new acknowledgement. In the convex region, used when CUBIC is not Reno-friendly and cwnd is at or above W_max, the window is increased by the same amount.

The Reno-friendly region exists because Reno performs well on short-RTT, small-bandwidth paths. The estimate of Reno's window, W_est, comes from the analysis of an additive-increase multiplicative-decrease algorithm with an additive factor alpha and a multiplicative factor beta, and it says alpha_cubic should be three times (1 minus beta_cubic) divided by (1 plus beta_cubic). On each new acknowledgement, if the cubic value is below W_est, CUBIC is in the Reno-friendly region and the window should be set to W_est. W_est is set to cwnd_epoch at the start of the stage and then updated on every new acknowledgement by adding alpha_cubic times segments_acked divided by cwnd. Once W_est has reached cwnd_prior, the sender should set alpha_cubic to 1 so that it can increase the window at the same rate as Reno, which uses AIMD(1, 0.5).

The convex region is also called the maximum probing phase, because CUBIC is searching for a new W_max. The network conditions may have changed since the last congestion event, perhaps because other flows left. The convex profile aims to increase the window very slowly at first, around W_max, and then to speed up gradually.
sections.plainLanguage: The window moves through three stages. On short paths it follows what Reno would do. Then it creeps up towards the size that caused the last loss. After that it curves away again, slowly at first, looking for a higher size that the network can now carry.

sections.title: Decrease, Fast Convergence, Timeout and Slow Start
sections.content:
When a congestion event is detected, CUBIC updates W_max and reduces cwnd and ssthresh immediately. On packet loss the sender must reduce both immediately on entering loss recovery, and beta_cubic should be set to 0.7, which differs from the factor used in the base TCP specification during fast recovery. The new slow start threshold is the flight size multiplied by beta_cubic, and the new congestion window is the larger of that threshold and two segments on loss, or one segment on an ECN-Echo signal, with the threshold itself at least two segments.

Using the flight size rather than cwnd matters when the application is rate limited: the amount of data in flight can be much smaller than cwnd, and reducing to a value based on cwnd would cut the window far more than needed. The mechanisms that manage cwnd and ssthresh during a rate-limited interval can be used instead. Implementations that keep using cwnd must use other measures to stop cwnd growing when fewer bytes are in flight than cwnd allows, which also stops it growing past the receive window. A QUIC sender that uses cwnd in this way is required to apply similar mechanisms.

Fast convergence is a heuristic for speeding up the way existing flows give up bandwidth to a new flow. When a congestion event occurs and the current cwnd is below W_max, W_max is reduced further, to cwnd multiplied by one plus beta_cubic and then divided by two. That forces the flow to plateau earlier and so lengthens the time it takes to grow again, leaving the new flow more time to catch up. In a network with only a single CUBIC flow and no other traffic, fast convergence should be disabled.

On a timeout, CUBIC follows Reno in reducing cwnd but sets the slow start threshold using beta_cubic, which differs from Reno. During the first congestion avoidance stage after a timeout, the window is increased with the cubic function with K set to zero and W_max set to the window size at the start of that stage, and W_est is set to that same size.

Slow start uses HyStart++ or, in rare cases where that is not suitable, the Reno slow start. When CUBIC uses HyStart++ it may leave the first slow start without any packet loss, so W_max is undefined; in that case CUBIC sets cwnd_prior to cwnd and switches to congestion avoidance with K set to zero and W_max set to the current window size.
sections.plainLanguage: On a loss the window is cut to 0.7 of the amount of data actually in flight, which avoids cutting too much when the application was sending slowly. A second rule makes old flows back off a little further when a new flow arrives, so the new one has room to grow.

sections.title: Spurious Congestion Events
sections.content:
When CUBIC reduces its window after detecting loss through duplicate acknowledgements or a timeout, the missing acknowledgement may arrive after the reduction and the retransmission. Packet reordering can trigger this, and a high degree of reordering can cause several window reductions, where spurious losses are wrongly read as congestion signals and CUBIC's performance suffers badly.

For TCP there are two kinds of spurious event: spurious timeouts and spurious fast retransmits. In QUIC there are no spurious timeouts, because the loss is only detected after an acknowledgement arrives.

An implementation may detect spurious timeouts with the mechanisms for Forward RTO-Recovery, and the Eifel detection algorithm is an experimental alternative. When a spurious timeout is detected, the implementation may follow the response algorithm that restores the congestion control state and adapts the retransmission timer to avoid further spurious timeouts.

Spurious fast retransmits can be detected on receiving an acknowledgement, either with TCP Timestamps or with D-SACK. The document specifies a simple response: save the current values of the window, the prior window, the slow start threshold, W_max, K, t_epoch and W_est before the window is reduced. Once the loss is confirmed to be spurious, CUBIC may restore those saved values if the current window is below cwnd_prior, which keeps performance close to what it would have been without the spurious loss. If the detection happens long after the event and the window has already grown past cwnd_prior, CUBIC should keep the current and most recent values.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets can arrive out of order, and a missing acknowledgement can turn up after the window has already been cut. The document allows the sender to notice that the loss was not real and put the window back where it was.

sections.title: Fairness and Scalability
sections.content:
With a deterministic loss model where the number of packets between two successive losses is always one divided by the loss rate, CUBIC always operates with the concave window profile, which simplifies the analysis. The document gives a formula for the average window size in that case, reduces it with beta_cubic set to 0.7, and then uses it to choose the value of C.

C determines how aggressive CUBIC is in competing with other algorithms for bandwidth. A lower value makes CUBIC friendlier to Reno, but a very low value such as 0.04 stops CUBIC using bandwidth efficiently on fast and long-distance networks. Based on tables of average window sizes for Reno, HighSpeed TCP and CUBIC at different round-trip times and loss rates, and on deployment experience, C = 0.4 is recommended as a balance between Reno-friendliness and aggressiveness of the window increase.

Those tables also show that CUBIC is friendlier to Reno than HighSpeed TCP, especially on short-RTT networks where Reno performs reasonably well. They also show that CUBIC uses spare bandwidth: to reach 10 Gbps, Reno TCP needs a packet loss rate of 2.0e-10 while CUBIC TCP needs 2.9e-8, and the cited test results indicate that CUBIC typically uses bandwidth left unused by existing Reno flows on the same bottleneck link without taking much bandwidth from them.

CUBIC has been studied with simulations, testbed emulations, Internet experiments and Internet measurements across a wide range of network environments, and these have demonstrated substantial benefits over classical Reno congestion control. Like Reno it is a loss-based algorithm, so because it is more aggressive it can fill large drop-tail buffers more quickly than Reno and increases the risk of a standing queue. Proper queue sizing and management can mitigate that risk to some extent. Its performance also suffers, as Reno's does, in networks where packet loss is not a good indication of bandwidth utilisation, such as wireless and mobile networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables in the document compare the average window each algorithm reaches at different loss rates. CUBIC is close to Reno on short paths and far ahead on long ones. The constant C decides how far ahead, and the document recommends 0.4.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: CUBIC makes no changes to the underlying security of a transport protocol and inherits the general security concerns described for TCP. Changing the window computation on the sender may let an attacker, by dropping or injecting acknowledgements, force the implementation to reduce its bandwidth or convince it that there is no congestion when there is, and use the implementation as an attack vector against other hosts. These attacks are not new to CUBIC and are inherent in any transport protocol like TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: CUBIC changes how fast a sender sends, not how the connection is protected. An attacker who can drop or forge acknowledgements can already misuse any TCP implementation, and CUBIC inherits that weakness.
